title: Given two strings, find the length of the longest subsequence common to both, where a subsequence keeps relative order but need not be contiguous. Explain the Longest Common Substring DP pattern applied to subsequences, the recurrence, the complexity, and a banking use case.
shortTitle: Longest Common Subsequence (Longest Ordered Sequence Shared by Two Strings)

s1_definition.profdef: The Longest Common Subsequence is the subsequence form of the Longest Common Substring pattern. We fill a two dimensional table where an entry is the length of the longest common subsequence of the two prefixes: on a character match it is one plus the diagonal, and on a mismatch it carries forward the better of the cell above or the cell to the left. The answer sits in the far corner. This runs in quadratic time and space.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India compares a customer's historical spending category sequence against a reference lifestyle pattern to see how closely they align in order, allowing gaps. The longest in-order overlap, even with skipped items, measures the similarity.
s1_definition.oneliner: On a match add one to the diagonal, on a mismatch keep the larger of the top or left neighbour.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** The Longest Common Subsequence is the subsequence form of the Longest Common Substring pattern. We fill a two dimensional table where an entry is the length of the longest common subsequence of the two prefixes: on a character match it is one plus the diagonal, and on a mismatch it carries forward the better of the cell above or the cell to the left. The answer sits in the far corner. This runs in quadratic time and space.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The National Bank of India compares a customer's historical spending category sequence against a reference lifestyle pattern to see how closely they align in order, allowing gaps. The longest in-order overlap, even with skipped items, measures the similarity.

**One line to remember:** On a match add one to the diagonal, on a mismatch keep the larger of the top or left neighbour.

sections.s2_technical:
We define the table entry for prefixes of length i and j as the length of the longest common subsequence of those prefixes. When the current characters match, that shared character extends the best subsequence of the shorter prefixes, so the entry is one plus the diagonal cell. When they differ, the last character of one prefix cannot help, so we take the better of dropping it, which is the cell above, or dropping the other, which is the cell to the left. Unlike the substring version, a mismatch never resets, it carries the best result forward.

Bottom-up: `for (int i = 1; i <= m; i++) for (int j = 1; j <= n; j++) dp[i][j] = a.charAt(i-1) == b.charAt(j-1) ? 1 + dp[i-1][j-1] : Math.max(dp[i-1][j], dp[i][j-1]);` and the answer is `dp[m][n]`. A concrete check: comparing GROCERY and GAMERY the longest common subsequence is GRY or GEY of length three. Senior nuance: this is quadratic in time and space, the answer is in the corner because a subsequence can span the whole prefixes, and you reconstruct the actual subsequence by walking back from the corner following matches and the larger neighbour.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India compares a customer's historical spending category sequence against a reference lifestyle pattern to measure how closely the customer's ordering of categories aligns with the pattern, allowing skipped categories, because a strong ordered overlap feeds a lifestyle segmentation model. Checking every subsequence is exponential. This is exactly how the Longest Common Subsequence works: it finds the longest in-order overlap in quadratic time with the match-extends-diagonal, mismatch-keeps-best recurrence.

The code defines a `SpendingAlignService` exposing `longestOrderedOverlap(a, b)` returning the length of the longest common subsequence. A `Demo` runs it over two sample category strings and logs the length.

sections.s5_journey:
The inputs are GROCERY and GAMERY. We want the longest in-order overlap allowing gaps.

Step 1 — We align GROCERY down the rows and GAMERY across the columns, with the border cells all zero.

Step 2 — The leading G matches G, so that cell becomes one plus its zero diagonal, giving one. This one propagates rightward and downward as a carried best.

Step 3 — Later the R in GROCERY meets the R in GAMERY and matches, extending a diagonal to two where the preceding G overlap was one.

Step 4 — The E meets E and the Y meets Y, each matching and extending the carried best. Mismatched cells in between simply keep the larger of their top or left neighbour, never resetting.

Step 5 — The corner cell ends at three, the length of an overlap such as G, then R or E, then Y. The answer is three. The output is below.

```
Oct 27, 2026 9:22:48 PM com.bank.spendalign.service.SpendingAlignService longestOrderedOverlap
INFO: Longest ordered spending overlap = 3
Oct 27, 2026 9:22:48 PM com.bank.spendalign.SpendingAlignApplication main
INFO: Ordered overlap length between category strings is 3
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  Input: a = "GROCERY", b = "GAMERY"
    │
    ▼
  dp[i][j]: match → 1 + diagonal, mismatch → max(top, left)
    │ G==G → 1 (carried forward)
    │ R==R → 2
    │ E==E, Y==Y → 3
    ▼
  Output: corner dp[m][n] = 3  (e.g. G,R,Y)
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
The Longest Common Subsequence is the subsequence form of the Longest Common Substring pattern, and I picture it as a grid with one string down the rows and the other across the columns, where each cell holds the longest common subsequence length of the two prefixes up to that point. When the current characters match, that shared character extends the best subsequence of the smaller prefixes, so the cell is one plus the diagonal. When they differ, I carry forward the larger of the cell above or the cell to the left, dropping whichever last character does not help.

The crucial difference from the substring version is that a mismatch never resets to zero, it carries the best result forward, which is why the final answer lives in the far corner of the table rather than at some maximum in the middle. This is quadratic in time and space, and I can reconstruct the actual subsequence by walking back from the corner, stepping diagonally on matches and toward the larger neighbour otherwise.

At the National Bank of India I used this to compare a customer's historical spending category sequence against a reference lifestyle pattern, allowing skipped categories, because a strong ordered overlap fed a lifestyle segmentation model. I filled the prefix table and read the corner value. Explaining the match-extends-diagonal and mismatch-keeps-best recurrence, why the answer is in the corner, and how it contrasts with the resetting substring version is what convinces an interviewer I understand the subsequence form of the Longest Common Substring pattern.
